item.title: Getting started
item.description:
Requirements

  • Hugo Extended, 0.128.0 or newer (the extended build, for image processing and Sass-free Hugo Pipes).
  • Git, for installation as a submodule or Hugo module.
  • Nothing else. There is no npm, no bundler and no external scripts; the theme builds with Hugo alone.

Installation as a Git submodule

From an existing Hugo site’s repository root:

git submodule add https://github.com/OWNER/radiance themes/radiance

Then set the theme in the site configuration:

# hugo.toml
theme = "radiance"

Installation as a Hugo module

hugo mod get github.com/OWNER/radiance

item.title: Appearance and colour schemes
item.description:
The toggle

The top panel carries one compact appearance control at its far right. With two colour schemes installed it swaps between them; with three or more it opens a small menu instead. The control is marked with aria-pressed (two schemes) or opens a menu with the current scheme marked, so the state never relies on the glyph alone.

With no stored choice the site follows the operating system through prefers-color-scheme, including live changes. An explicit choice is stored in localStorage under the single key radiance-appearance and applied before first paint by the generated inline scheme-init script, so there is no flash of the wrong scheme. If storage is blocked the choice still applies to the current page. Nothing is sent to a server.

item.title: Making it yours
item.description:
Site name

Set title in hugo.toml. It appears as the panel title (linking home), in window and dialog text, in the footer and in feed metadata.

Navigation

The panel reads one primary menu, main:

[[menus.main]]
  name = "Posts"
  pageRef = "/posts"
  weight = 10

Entries render left to right by weight, and only when the menu has entries — a site with no menu renders none. The current section is marked with aria-current. One entry parameter is supported:

item.title: Writing
item.description:
Posts

Ordinary Markdown pages render in a window with the title, the date, taxonomy links and the body:

---
title: "My first post"
date: 2026-01-17
description: "A one-line summary used in listings and social cards."
tags: ["journal"]
categories: ["general"]
---

Your text here.

description is optional but recommended: listings and the Open Graph fallback use it, falling back to a truncated plain-text summary.

Images and captions

The theme adds no shortcodes; posts are plain Markdown. Reference images the ordinary way:

item.title: Photography
item.description:
What the theme does with images

The theme processes images only in two places — moodboard image tiles and social-card covers — and always with Hugo’s built-in imaging, so no external service is involved.

Moodboard image tiles receive three WebP variants (480, 800 and 1200 pixels wide) served through a srcset, with intrinsic dimensions, lazy loading and asynchronous decoding. SVG files are never resized.

Covers (the cover front matter field on moodboards) are resized to a 1200-pixel-wide JPEG for Open Graph and Twitter cards. An SVG cover is passed through untouched.

item.title: Moodboards
item.description:
Creating a board

A moodboard is a page bundle under content/moodboards/. Scaffold one:

hugo new --kind moodboards content/moodboards/my-board

This creates index.md, tiles.yaml and images/placeholder.png. The section page uses layout: moodboard-list; each board’s index.md uses layout: moodboard.

Board front matter

Field Required Purpose
title yes Window title and list entry.
description no Concise preview in the list; also the social summary.
date no Page metadata; used by the archive and search.
weight no Ordering in the moodboards list.
tiles no Resource filename holding the tile list; default tiles.yaml.
palette no List of validated hex colours, appended as a palette tile.
cover no Resource filename; list preview and social card image.

Tiles

The tile list is the board’s own bundle resource — never global site data — and is a YAML list. Every tile has a type, an optional span (1x1 default, 2x1 or 2x2) and type-specific fields. The complete type table lives in the theme’s data/tiles.yaml and is rendered in the reference appendix; in brief:

item.title: Customising
item.description:
Template overrides

Every partial and layout can be overridden from the site: create the same path under your site’s layouts/ directory and Hugo uses yours. Common overrides:

  • layouts/partials/footer.html — footer text;
  • layouts/partials/desktop-icons.html — replace the data-driven shortcut column with your own markup;
  • layouts/_default/single.html — wrap post bodies differently.

Partials that take parameters document them in a leading template comment; keep to that contract when you override.

Styles

The theme concatenates its stylesheets (including the generated scheme CSS) and links them in partials/head.html. To add site-specific CSS without touching the theme, override head.html and append your own Hugo Pipes resources after the theme’s links. Two rules from the theme still apply to your styles:

item.title: Publishing and maintenance
item.description:
Deployment

The theme emits a plain static site into public/; any static host works. Two things keep it portable:

  • all URLs are Hugo-generated or relURL-resolved, so the site deploys below a subpath unchanged;
  • no remote assets are fetched at build time or run time, so the build is reproducible on CI.

GitHub Pages

The demo repository deploys to GitHub Pages with Actions. The shape of that workflow is: check out the repository (with submodules), install Hugo Extended, run hugo --source exampleSite --themesDir ../.. and publish exampleSite/public as the artifact. A complete guardrail workflow ships with the theme in .github/workflows/; it also fails the build on the checks listed in the reference appendix’s maintenance notes.

item.description: This appendix is generated from the theme’s data files at build time — the tables below are never transcribed by hand.

item.title: Who Radiance is for, and who it isn't
item.description:
Who it is for

Radiance suits people publishing for themselves:

  • Personal homepages — a place that says who you are, what you are making and how to reach you.
  • Blogs — ordinary posts in ordinary windows, with an archive, tags and search that need no configuration beyond a content file.
  • Photography and sketch journals — images framed and processed by the theme, in moodboards or in plain post bodies.
  • Collections — moodboards of links, notes, palettes and sounds for anything you gather.

The desktop chrome is the point: it is nostalgic, small, quick and a little playful, and the site remains an ordinary website — links, scrolling, bookmarks.

item.title: Appendix: telling people about it
item.description:
A factual checklist for distributing the theme. Nothing here is a promise of results; it is the list of places that make sense and the preparation each one needs.

Hugo themes gallery

The theme’s theme.toml already carries the metadata the gallery lists: name, licence, description, minimum Hugo version, tags and features. Before submitting, replace the OWNER placeholders with the real repository path, confirm the live demo URL and check the gallery’s submission guidance for screenshot requirements.

item.title: A week on the Skye trail
item.description: I did not expect to come back with any photographs at all. The forecast for the week read like a dare — five days of “showers”, two of “rain” — and Skye does not need encouragement to live up to it. But the weather on the island moves faster than the forecast, and between the fronts the light arrived in short, unbelievable bursts.

item.title: Design tokens
item.description:
All authored colour values in radiance live in the scheme files under data/schemes/ — one YAML file per scheme. A generated stylesheet turns the scheme data into custom properties; every other stylesheet refers to those properties, for example:

a {
  color: var(--accent-link);
}

Starting palette

The starting palette takes its cues from Ubuntu’s Radiance theme:

  • Dark compact panels with fine borders.
  • A deep aubergine desktop with a warm orange glow.
  • An orange focus accent and a darker orange for links.

These are starting values, not a guarantee of accessible contrast; scripts/contrast.py checks the documented pairs and fails when body text drops below 4.5:1 or borders and focus rings below 3:1.

item.title: Getting started
item.description:
Prerequisites

radiance needs Hugo Extended 0.128.0 or newer. Check the installed version:

hugo version

Build the example site

The theme repository ships an example site:

hugo --source exampleSite --themesDir ../..

The command assumes the theme checkout directory is named radiance, so that ../.. resolves from exampleSite to the directory containing the theme.

Next steps

  • Read the other sample post listed under Posts.
  • Adjust the colours in data/schemes/radiance.yaml.

item.title: About this site
item.description:
This example site demonstrates radiance, a Hugo theme that makes a content website feel like an Ubuntu desktop running GNOME 2.

The theme

  • The default light appearance is inspired by Ubuntu Radiance.
  • The Ambiance dark appearance is its darker companion.
  • All authored colour values live in the scheme files under data/schemes/.

This site

The top panel carries the site title, the primary navigation links, a search link and the appearance toggle. The sample posts cover getting started and the design tokens.

item.title: Work with me
item.description:
This page is a case study in the shape of a decision log — the record of how radiance was designed and, just as importantly, what was removed from it. It is self-initiated work: nobody commissioned this theme; it exists because a desktop metaphor seemed worth building properly and then worth cutting back honestly.

The original concept

The first sketch was a desktop simulator: pages as windows that could be minimised, maximised and closed; a bottom panel with a window list, four workspaces and a trash; state kept in session storage so your windows came back when you returned. It was fun to build and, for about a week, fun to use.
